opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
I am so glad to be reading the readings. I only desire to do it daily, but my weakness has me prisoner to every second of sleep. So today, with a little room before I needed to leave, I read the readings.
I then realize how the daily readings are just a piece of the many pieces of the Bible’s message from the Old Covenant to the New. Today was no different. I had to read these readings, so I ponder. You would think you would not ponder on readings already read two or thirty times, but not true. So much is revealed each time.
Today, I never noticed, “For by faith He purified their hearts.” Or when Jesus tells His disciples, “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in His love.” Then again, “I have told you this so that my joy might be in you and your joy might be complete.”
First, what exactly are His Father’s commandments? Aren’t those the commandments inscribed through Moses and revealed to the first generation after the departure from Egypt, when our mighty Father revealed the plan? I say “first generation” because the plan had already been moving through generations prior, yet during that time, something was becoming realized before humanity.
But back to the Father’s commandments. Jesus specifically says, “Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments.” Moments earlier, He tells them, “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love.” Are they different commandments? Is Jesus’ instruction from the Father different than what was given to us? Or is He revealing that they are not separate at all? That He remains in His Father’s love, and we remain in His love, because the love itself is the same.
Perhaps this is why Christ speaks the way He does. Not to separate Himself from the Father, but to reveal that only through Him can we enter into that same relationship of love.
I think some people might say it is silly to get hung up on statements and sentences like this. But Scripture is words that are living. Think about that… living words. What does that even mean?
For me, these words are incarnate of Christ. They represent His life and somehow do not end in His death. They continue through the Resurrection and beyond it. It is almost as if the Gospel rushed from the beginning toward the end, yet after the Resurrection, humanity was left in a kind of “stay tuned” moment. A waiting period. A refining period. And while in this waiting, Christ tells us to remain in His commandments so as to remain in His love.
But then what is “that moment” we are waiting for?
I often think about the world ending. I think there will be an ending and somehow a beginning within it. But time, as we know it, is not of God. Time traps humanity, yet God exists outside of what governs us. So how do eternity and time coexist? And does humanity misunderstand what fulfillment even is?
Then I return again to Christ’s words: “I have told you this so that my joy might be in you and your joy might be complete.” Complete.
There is not a day that goes by that I do not fracture one of the commandments. I do not kill, per se, but I can become angry, truly angry over simple things. And Christ Himself reveals that the roots matter too. The outward act is not the only measure. Anger is not murder literally, yet it comes from the same fractured nature. That realization is uncomfortable because it removes our ability to stand proudly beside the commandments as though we have perfectly kept them.
And yet Christ does not say, “Achieve perfection and then come to me.” He says, “Remain in my love.”
That changes everything.
Because maybe humanity becomes so focused on sin, on failure, on constantly measuring fractures, that we miss what Christ is actually saying. Not that sin does not matter, because it does. Not that we should stop fighting against it, because we must. But perhaps our joy does not come from obsessing over our inability to perfect ourselves. Perhaps joy comes from remaining in the One who already remains perfectly in the Father’s love.
Maybe that is why He says, “My joy might be in you, and your joy might be complete.” Not future tense only. Not merely at the end of the world. But now. Through Him.
So perhaps completion is not humanity finally reaching a state where no fracture remains. Perhaps completion begins the moment we stop trying to stand before God through our own strength and instead remain in the love Christ is already offering us.
And if Christ already remains perfectly in the Father’s love, and invites us to remain in Him, then when we stand before God in the end, will He first ask us how perfectly we conquered our sinful nature… or whether we truly believed the completeness of His love was enough to remain in it?
